content: 1. Pesticides that are legally restricted to use by trained or registered operators must not be advertised to the general public, except through specialized journals targeting such operators. If advertised, the restricted availability must be clearly and prominently displayed. 2. Advertising must not promote uses of pesticides that are not specified on the approved label. 3. Promotional materials must not include recommendations that contradict national regulatory decisions. 4. Claims regarding safety, such as safe, non-poisonous, harmless, non-toxic, environmentally friendly, or compatible with IPM/IVM, must not appear on labels, pamphlets, or other publicity materials, even with qualifying phrases like when used as directed. However, references to use within validated IPM/IVM programs may be included if approved by the regulatory authority and appropriately qualified. 5. Advertisements must not depict unsafe practices, such as mixing or applying pesticides without adequate protective clothing, using pesticides near food, or using them in the presence of or near children. 6. Advertising and promotional materials must highlight appropriate warning phrases and symbols as outlined in the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) and FAO/WHO labeling guidelines. 7. Advertisements and promotional activities must not include inappropriate incentives or gifts to encourage the purchase of pesticides. 8. Pesticide laws should establish specific requirements for pesticide advertising, define advertising broadly to cover all forms, designate the authority responsible for enforcement, and prohibit the advertising of unregistered or illegal pesticides, false or misleading claims, and advertising contrary to approved uses or label instructions. 9. Pesticide storage is regulated under both pesticide legislation and other legal instruments addressing hazardous substances or chemicals. Regulators must consider all relevant legislation before drafting storage provisions in pesticide laws. 10. Pesticide legislation should provide general storage requirements applicable to all pesticide storage and may establish additional requirements for large quantities or specific categories of products. These provisions may include safety measures and restrictions on storage locations to minimize risks, particularly in residential areas, near hospitals, schools, or waterways. 11. Facilities storing large quantities of pesticides must meet stringent conditions, such as impermeable flooring, emergency access, firefighting equipment, ventilation, and secure storage records and safety data sheets. 12. Specific procedures are required for obsolete pesticide stocks in storage. Entities with such stocks must notify the responsible authority with details of the amounts, types, locations, and ages of the products. The authority will determine the best course of action based on available disposal options. 13. The transport of pesticides and pesticide-related waste may be regulated under pesticide legislation or broader national laws addressing hazardous substances. If no general transportation law exists, pesticide laws should include basic transport provisions. 14. Vehicles and containers used for pesticide transport must meet specific requirements, and pesticides must not be transported with passengers, animals, food, or feed. If joint transport is unavoidable, adequate physical separation must be ensured to prevent contamination. 15. Vehicles carrying bulk quantities of pesticides must display hazard placards and carry Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) or Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for the products. 16. Legislation must address procedures for pesticide accidents or spillages during transport, including immediate notification of the responsible authority. 17. The disposal of pesticides and pesticide-related waste must comply with instructions from the designated national authority. Illegal dumping, pouring pesticides into water sources, burying waste, or burning waste (except in approved incinerators) must be prohibited. 18. Exceptions may be made for certain containers that are rinsed in specific ways and can be disposed of in ordinary landfills. 19. Legislation should include provisions for phasing out banned or deregistered pesticides, requiring inventories of obsolete stocks, and promoting proper stock management to prevent accumulation. 20. Disposal and remediation of contaminated sites must occur in an environmentally sound manner, as established in the legislation. This may involve broader environmental or hazardous substance laws. 21. The Basel Convention applies to the disposal of hazardous wastes, including obsolete pesticides, and requires proper documentation, prior consent from transit countries, and adherence to packaging, labeling, and transport requirements. 22. The Stockholm Convention addresses the management of stockpiles, waste, and contaminated sites containing Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) and requires that POPs content be destroyed or irreversibly transformed into non-POPs. 23. Pesticide companies are encouraged to assist in the environmentally sound disposal of banned or obsolete pesticides and used containers. 24. Legislation should designate the responsible authority for regulating, monitoring, and enforcing provisions related to pesticide storage, transport, and disposal. 25. Information collection and monitoring are essential for understanding pesticide risks, usage trends, and incidents. This data informs policy decisions, public awareness campaigns, and regulatory actions. 26. Authorities may require manufacturers, importers, distributors, and sellers to maintain records for a specified period to support monitoring and enforcement efforts.
